question: A 55-year-old construction worker falls off a 2-story scaffolding and injures his back. His coworkers bring him to the urgent care clinic within 30 minutes of the fall. He complains of left lower-limb weakness and loss of sensation in the right lower limb. He does not have any past medical history. His vital signs are stable. A neurologic examination reveals a total loss of motor function when testing left knee extension, along with the left-sided loss of light touch sensation from the mid-thigh and below. There is a right-sided loss of pin-prick sensation of the lateral leg and entire foot. At this time of acute injury, what other finding is most likely to be found in this patient?

options.opa: Left-sided numbness at the level of the lesion
options.opd: Right-sided loss of proprioception and vibration sensation
options.ope: Left-sided spastic paralysis below the lesion

reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Fall from height" -> "Back injury" -> "Spinal cord injury" -> "Hemisection of spinal cord" -> "Brown-Séquard syndrome" -> "Ipsilateral motor loss" -> "Contralateral sensory loss" -> "Left-sided spastic paralysis below the lesion" -> 85%

enhanced_information: The patient likely has Brown-Séquard syndrome due to a spinal cord hemisection from the fall. This condition typically results in ipsilateral motor loss and proprioception/vibration sensation loss, along with contralateral pain and temperature sensation loss. The patient's symptoms of left lower-limb weakness and right-sided loss of pin-prick sensation align with this syndrome. In the acute phase of spinal cord injury, spastic paralysis may not yet be evident due to spinal shock, which initially causes flaccid paralysis. Therefore, the most likely finding at this time is an extensor plantar response on the left side, indicating an upper motor neuron lesion. The retrieved evidence path confirms the association between spinal cord injury and Brown-Séquard syndrome, supporting the diagnosis. Thus, the correct answer is 'Left-sided extensor plantar response.'
analysis: The patient's symptoms are consistent with Brown-Séquard syndrome, which results from a hemisection of the spinal cord. This condition typically presents with ipsilateral motor loss and proprioception/vibration sensation loss, along with contralateral pain and temperature sensation loss. In this case, the patient exhibits left lower-limb weakness and right-sided loss of pin-prick sensation, aligning with the syndrome. In the acute phase of spinal cord injury, spinal shock can cause flaccid paralysis, but an extensor plantar response (Babinski sign) may still be present, indicating an upper motor neuron lesion. Therefore, the most likely finding at this time is a left-sided extensor plantar response.
